newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Asian rights group critices Indonesian poll.
newsitem.headline: Asian rights group critices Indonesian poll.

text.p: An Asian-based human rights group issued a critical report on the Indonesian election on Saturday, saying glaring irregularities had undermined the right to vote.

The Bangkok-based Asian Forum for Human Rights and Development said in a statement issued by a delegation visiting Indonesia for Thursday's poll that they had basic concerns with irregularities in the electoral process.

The group's mission coordinator, Evelyn Balais-Serrano, told a news conference that the group with delegates from Thailand, the Philippines and Cambodia had been surprised by the level of the military presence in and around polling booths.
"We think there can never be a clear and fair election in an atmosphere of fear," Balais-Serrano told reporters in issuing the group's three-page statement on the poll.
"We express grave alarm that the peoples of Indonesia should so suffer violations of their sacred right to vote freely without fear or reprisal," the group said in the statement.

"While the government speaks of a registered list of voters amounting to some 124 plus million, election authorities in some areas did not seem to mind the list at all in allowing citizens to vote," the statement said.

It said some of the seven-member delegation spread across the archipelago had seen people vote without their names being checked off a registered list and no mechanism to ensure electors voting out of their districts did not vote more than once.
The report was critical of the tight restrictions on campaign at the village level where most of Indonesia's population of more than 200 million live.

"Observations, interviews and reports showed that one party, the ruling party of Golkar had full access and control over the villages as each village head was a member of Golkar. How can the people have a free and fair choice under such circumstances."
The group was also concerned about the pressure on the more than 20 million young voters taking part in the election for the first time.

"Interviews with young voters and their parents in Jakarta and some other areas showed with glaring frequency fear among the young that failure to vote for Golkar would mean reprisal by their superiors in school involving their academic work, such as a failing mark, for instance, in their final examinations," it said.
The forum urged the Indonesian government to set up an independent election body with a transparent electoral process free from harassment and intimidation.
